section: 1.  Identify the most‐recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_in: one file on disk in script_dir/results
grain_out: one row per CSV file whose name matches the pattern, carrying path, base and date
units_out: file paths and parsed dates; no measured quantity
operation: Lists the results directory, keeps only names of the form base_YYYY-MM-DD.csv for nine hardcoded bases, and splits each name into a base and a date. The second filter on base %in% base_names is absorbed because it only re-applies the restriction the regex already imposed.
settings: Nine bases fixed in code: population_invariability, community_invariability, portfolio_ps, synchrony_ps, L5_alpha_diversity_observed, L5_gamma_diversity_observed, L5_beta_diversity_observed, beta_bray_pairs_monthly, beta_bray_bay_period_season. Date must match \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} immediately before .csv, anchored at both ends. Non-recursive listing; results_dir fixed as script_dir/results.
na_behavior: If nothing matches, all_csv is empty and files_df has zero rows, with no error raised here. str_extract cannot fail given the regex, but a pattern-valid impossible date such as 2026-13-40 becomes NA in as.Date silently; downstream an NA date is indistinguishable from a date that simply sorted last.

section: 1.  Identify the most‐recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_in: one row per matching CSV file
grain_out: one row per base name, being the single file chosen to represent that base
operation: Sorts by base, then date descending, then file name descending, and keeps the first row per base so each base resolves to exactly one file. The missing-base warning block is absorbed because it only reports on the selection just made.
settings: arrange(base, desc(date), desc(fname)); slice_head(n = 1); ties on date broken by reverse alphabetical file name; a base with no file produces warning() rather than an error, so execution continues.
na_behavior: dplyr::arrange places NA dates last, so a file with an unparseable date is selected only when it is the only file for its base. A base with no file is silently absent from latest_per_base and appears only in the warning text; the consequence surfaces later as an object-not-found error at the rename step.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
grain_in: one row per base (a file path)
grain_out: a named list, then separate data frames in the global environment, each keeping the grain of its own file; only pop_inv is consumed later in this script
units_out: mixed, as stored in each file; for pop_inv the invariability index I_i
operation: Reads each selected CSV with readr::read_csv, deframes to a named list, pushes the list into the global environment, and copies the objects under shorter working names. The list2env call, the nine renames and the rm cleanup are absorbed because they change names and environment contents only, not what a row means. The region crosses the section 3 header, and eight of the nine tables are loaded but never used in this script.
settings: show_col_types = FALSE, so column types are guessed from the first 1000 rows and the guess is not printed. keep_objs decides what survives the rm. beta_bray is taken from beta_bray_bay_period_season and beta_bray_montn (spelled without the i of monthly) from beta_bray_pairs_monthly.
na_behavior: read_csv maps empty fields, the literal string NA, and values that do not parse into the guessed column type onto the same NA, and problems() is never inspected, so those three causes are not distinguishable downstream. If a base failed to resolve in the previous node, its rename line raises an error and the script stops there.

grain_in: one row of pop_inv. Open question: the comment block at lines 223 to 229 states that pop_inv rows are indexed by major_area, period and season and that the key column is mean_invariability, but the model consumes I_i and species_code, which implies a finer grain of species x bay x season and possibly x period. Which description is correct cannot be determined from this script.
grain_out: one fitted model object: seasonal fixed effects plus two variance components and their conditional modes
units_in: invariability index I_i (mean squared over variance, dimensionless)
units_out: log10 index units for fixed and random effects; squared log10 units for variance components
operation: Fits a linear mixed model of log10(I_i) on season with random intercepts for bay and for species, then prints the summary and the bay conditional modes; the two printing calls are absorbed because they display the fit and produce nothing new. No positivity filter on I_i is applied here, unlike the figure that begins at fig_pop_season <- pop_inv %>%.
settings: REML by default. Season enters as a factor with the first level as reference, alphabetically Fall unless the CSV column arrived as an ordered factor or the levels were set elsewhere. Random intercepts only, no random slopes and no correlation terms. No weights, no offset. Default optimizer and convergence tolerances. lmerTest is attached, so the summary reports Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Default na.action = na.omit. Period, named in the pop_inv comment block, is not in the model.
na_behavior: Rows with NA in any model variable are dropped without notice. log10 of a negative I_i yields NaN and is dropped the same way, so missing I_i, missing season, missing bay, missing species code and non-positive I_i all collapse into a single count that appears only in the printed summary line about observations deleted due to missingness, and is not stored anywhere. log10 of exactly zero yields -Inf, which is not NA and is not dropped; it would make the fit fail rather than shrink. Nothing in the script checks whether pop_inv contains zero or negative I_i.

grain_out: one box per season summarising the retained rows as median, quartiles and whiskers
operation: Keeps rows with I_i strictly greater than zero and draws boxplots of log10(I_i) by season. Recorded as a node because the filter changes which population is described relative to the model at m_pop, which applies no such filter, so the figure and the model can describe different sets of rows.
settings: Threshold I_i > 0, strict, so exact zeros are excluded. Boxplot fill alpha 0.7. Default ggplot whiskers at 1.5 times the interquartile range with points beyond drawn as outliers. Legend suppressed. No explicit season ordering, so seasons appear in the column's existing factor order or alphabetically.
na_behavior: filter also removes rows where I_i is NA, since NA > 0 evaluates to NA, so missing values and non-positive values leave by the same door and neither is counted or reported. The number of rows behind each box is not shown.

end_context: fig_bay_re <- ggplot(bay_re, aes(x = estimate, y = level)) +
grain_out: one row per bay (major_area level), each with a conditional mode and an interval; then one plotted point and error bar per bay
units_out: deviation in log10 invariability units, with an interval on the same scale
operation: Extracts the random effect values from the fit, keeps only the major_area intercepts, and plots each bay against a reference line at zero. The ggplot block is absorbed because it displays this quantity and creates no new one.
settings: effects = "ran_vals" returns conditional modes (BLUPs), which are shrunk toward zero and are not group means. conf.int = TRUE gives a Wald interval from the conditional standard deviation at the 95% default, which treats the variance components as known. Filters group == "major_area" and term == "(Intercept)". Error bar height 0.2, dashed grey reference line at 0, no ordering of levels by estimate so bays appear in factor order.
na_behavior: No missing values are expected while the model converges. A singular or non-converged fit still yields estimates and intervals here, and nothing checks for that. A bay whose rows were all dropped in the fit never appears as a level, and its absence for that reason cannot be told apart from a bay that was never in the data.

grain_out: one row per retained species code, at most 30, being the 15 lowest and 15 highest intercepts
units_out: deviation in log10 invariability units, with an interval on the same scale
operation: Extracts the species intercepts, sorts them ascending, and keeps every species when there are 30 or fewer, otherwise the 15 smallest and the 15 largest. The factor releveling is absorbed because it only fixes plot order. The comment above the block says top 15 most extreme while the code keeps up to 30 species, 15 at each end.
settings: Cutoff at 30; 15 taken from each tail via slice(., c(1:15, (n_tot-14):n_tot)). For n_tot = 31 this drops exactly one middle species; for n_tot below 16 the two index ranges overlap and rows would be duplicated. Sorting is by estimate ascending with no explicit tie break, so ties keep the order tidy returned. Intervals are the same 95% Wald intervals as for the bay node.
na_behavior: No NA is introduced here. Species dropped from the fit, whether for missing I_i, a missing grouping variable or non-positive I_i, are absent from the level list, and absence for those reasons cannot be distinguished from a species that was never sampled.

grain_in: one row per retained species code
grain_out: one row per retained species code with a common name attached; the row count is unchanged only if the lookup holds at most one row per code
operation: Loads data.Rdata for the species lookup table and left joins common names onto the retained species codes, coercing both keys to character first; the two coercions and the select are absorbed because they only align key types and trim columns, while the join is the node. The load brings in every other object stored in data.Rdata and the script neither lists them nor guards against overwriting. data.Rdata is read from the working directory set by setwd(script_dir), not from results_dir, and it is not one of the dated files selected earlier, so its vintage is not tracked.
settings: left_join keyed by c("level" = "species_code"); only species_code and com_name are taken from the lookup. The closing mutate fixes factor levels to the joined row order, which is the estimate order inherited from the previous node.
na_behavior: A species code absent from the lookup receives com_name NA, silently and without a count. Because factor() drops NA from its levels, that row then carries an NA factor value and is removed at plotting time. If two retained species share a common name, or the lookup holds more than one row for a code, factor(com_name, levels = com_name) is handed duplicated levels and the call fails with an error; a duplicated code would also multiply rows in the join, which nothing checks.

start_anchor: fig_spec_re_c <- ggplot(spec_re2, aes(x = estimate, y = com_name)) +
grain_out: two figures, one point and interval per species in each, plus one TIFF file on disk
units_out: rendered figure; the saved file is an image, not a quantity
operation: Builds the species caterpillar plot labelled by common name and the same plot labelled by species code, prints all four figures when P equals 1, and writes only the common name version to results/Fig_S4_population_variability_600dpi.tif. No quantity changes meaning inside this region; it is listed as a node so that the export settings and the choice of which figure becomes the supplementary figure are visible to a reviewer rather than falling outside every region.
settings: P == 1 controls display only and does not gate the export. results_dir is recomputed as script_dir/results just before the save. TIFF at 27 by 15 cm (18 and 10.0 multiplied by 1.5), 600 dpi, lzw compression, white background. Error bar height 0, dashed reference line at 0, base font size 10 for the common name plot and 8 for the code plot. Only fig_spec_re_c is saved, under a name declaring it Fig_S4.
na_behavior: A species carrying NA com_name from the join is dropped by ggplot with a removed-rows warning that is easy to miss in console output, so the saved figure can hold fewer species than spec_re2 has rows. ggsave raises an error if results_dir does not exist, and overwrites an existing file of the same name without prompting.
